clue.text: They provide – and are provided with – leads?

definitions.text: They provide – and are provided with – leads?

blocks.note: surface reading: informants or detectives who supply leads, meaning clues in an investigation
setter's reading: animals that are put on leads, meaning leashes, while sniffing out evidence for officers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads' works twice: the tips an investigation follows, and the leashes these animals are walked on. The answer both finds clues and wears a leash.
explanation.definitionFit: Trained sniffer animals working with officers turn up evidence and are themselves kept on leashes.

clue.text: Suffer from sunburn in exercise the French offered up

indicators.note: in a down clue, something offered up is lifted upwards, so its letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school exercise
le is the French masculine word for 'the'

explanation.surface: Someone sunburnt during a workout given by a French instructor.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the French article flips; the PE stays as it is and sits on top of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunburnt skin flakes away in strips, which is what happens when a burnt person starts to shed it.

clue.text: German denied sportsmen's house is source of valuable deposits

indicators.note: to be denied something is to go without it, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for German
a lodge is a house used by hunters or anglers during the sporting season

explanation.surface: A German turned away from a hunting lodge that sits on a rich seam.
explanation.walkthrough: A shooting or fishing lodge is the country house sportsmen stay in; take the G out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lode is a vein of metal ore in rock, the natural seam miners dig for precious minerals.

clue.text: Firm belly

blocks.note: first meaning: a large company
second meaning: a dated humorous word for a pot belly

explanation.surface: A toned, flat stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as an adjective describing a toned stomach, but it is a noun meaning a business. The paunch sense is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a large business entity, and jokingly a prominent paunch, as a big body grows.

clue.text: Compactness in cavity when half's given up for animals' lairs

indicators.note: giving up one portion in exchange for something else is a swap, so half the word is replaced

blocks.note: a den is a wild animal's lair
taken as written; its first half, CAV, is the part surrendered

explanation.surface: Tightly packed earth inside a hollow where creatures make their homes.
explanation.walkthrough: The six-letter word splits into two halves of three; the front half goes and the lairs take its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Density measures how tightly matter is packed together, which is the quality of being compact.

clue.text: Who may wear pairs of spiked shoes, hoping to get a hole in one?

definitions.text: Who may wear pairs of spiked shoes, hoping to get a hole in one?

blocks.clueFragment: wear pairs of spiked shoes, hoping to get a hole in one
blocks.note: surface reading: someone in spiked shoes might expect a hole worn in one of them
setter's reading: the dream shot of a sportsman who wears cleats on the course

explanation.walkthrough: Spiked shoes suggest damage, so a 'hole in one' sounds like a puncture in a shoe; it is really a single stroke from tee to cup.
explanation.definitionFit: Players on the links wear studded shoes for grip, and every one of them dreams of an ace.

clue.text: High speed in section of film

blocks.note: first meaning: a fast pace
second meaning: a short extract from a movie

explanation.surface: A fast-motion sequence within a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are joined by 'in', which reads as part of a single phrase about filming.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a brisk rate of movement and also a short excerpt cut from a longer movie.

clue.text: Liquid preparation possessing traces of very erogenous powers, ostensibly?

definitions.text: Liquid preparation possessing traces of very erogenous powers, ostensibly?

indicators.note: a trace is the faintest sign of something, so only an opening letter of each word survives
to possess is to hold, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: a lotion is a liquid preparation applied to the skin
first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A tonic claimed to carry hints of powerful aphrodisiac effects.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a liquid that supposedly has erotic powers. 'Ostensibly' supplies a letter and also the doubt about whether it works.
explanation.definitionFit: A philtre is a drink supposed to make someone fall in love, so it claims aphrodisiac powers that are dubious.

clue.text: Boar with pearls: preposterous, they're savage beasts

indicators.note: something preposterous is absurdly out of order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Echoes the saying about casting pearls before swine: a wild pig decked in pearls is absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls 'pearls before swine', with the boar as the swine.
explanation.definitionFit: These large Arctic carnivores are among the most dangerous predators, so calling them fierce animals fits.

clue.text: In steadfast manner, underlying reforms

indicators.note: to reform something is to reshape it, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone firmly committed to the deep changes behind a programme of reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reforms' looks like a noun the fodder describes, but it is a verb acting on that fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in a lasting, persistent way is done with constancy that holds firm over time.

clue.text: Making comeback, survive wickedness

indicators.note: a comeback is a return journey, so the letters travel backwards

blocks.note: to live on is to survive

explanation.surface: A villain who returns from apparent defeat, as wickedness endures.
explanation.walkthrough: The word read backwards gives its own moral opposite, a favourite crossword reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name moral badness, the quality of being thoroughly bad or sinful.

clue.text: In which nameless prince cavorts during dip, robe abandoned?

definitions.text: In which nameless prince cavorts during dip, robe abandoned?

indicators.note: to be without a name is to lose the abbreviation for name, so a letter goes
to cavort is to leap about wildly, so the letters jump into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, before N for name is dropped
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A racy novel where an anonymous prince frolics in a skinny-dip, his robe cast aside.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for name. The whole clue also describes the genre: steamy romance featuring a disrobed nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: This term names a sexually charged historical romance novel, the kind where clothes come off in passion.

clue.text: Intellectual studying anatomy, audaciously clutching needle, experimenting with the optic nerve, primarily?

definitions.text: Intellectual studying anatomy, audaciously clutching needle, experimenting with the optic nerve, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.clueFragment: Intellectual studying anatomy, audaciously clutching needle, experimenting with the optic nerve
blocks.note: first letters of the eleven words

explanation.surface: A scholar investigating the eye by boldly poking a needle near the optic nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the physicist really did push a bodkin behind his own eyeball to study vision.
explanation.definitionFit: The great English physicist famously experimented on his own eye with a bodkin while researching optics and light.

clue.text: For every swearword, I initially overlay noisy drum sounds?

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only an opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: per means for each, as in 'ten pounds per head'
a cuss is a curse or swearword
taken as written
first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A musician swearing every time they cover up a loud drum track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I initially' looks like one phrase, but the I stands whole and 'initially' acts on the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Percussion is the striking of instruments such as drums, and the collective noise they make.

clue.text: '80s pop star's characteristic? Extreme frugality

blocks.note: first meaning, playful: the quality of being Sting, singer with the Police in the 1980s
second meaning: meanness with money

explanation.surface: A famous singer known for never picking up the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Sting is the stage name of the English singer of the Police; add '-iness' and the quality of being him becomes meanness.
explanation.definitionFit: Being excessively reluctant to spend or give money is miserliness, an exaggerated form of thrift.

clue.text: Second in Treasury dismissed before reshuffle, one with a big mouth

indicators.note: someone dismissed is sent away, so a letter leaves the word
a reshuffle rearranges ministers, so what remains is put in a new order

blocks.note: the word taken whole; its second letter, R, is the one sent away

explanation.surface: A junior Treasury minister sacked in a cabinet reshuffle, a loudmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second in Treasury' sounds like a deputy minister; it is just the second letter. 'One with a big mouth' seems to be a gossip but is geographical.
explanation.definitionFit: A river widens into a broad tidal outlet where it meets the sea, a river mouth in geography.

clue.text: Land around a Pacific port

indicators.note: to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: to settle is to come to rest, as a bird lands
taken as written

explanation.surface: Territory surrounding a harbour on the Pacific coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land' reads as a noun but works as a verb meaning come down to rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The city in Washington State sits on Puget Sound and is a major Pacific shipping harbour.

clue.text: Packaging manufacturer, one's penetrating, more astute

indicators.note: to penetrate is to get inside, so one piece enters the other

blocks.note: a canner packs food into tins
one is I, the Roman numeral; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: An insider at a packaging company proves sharper than rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: Canny is a Scots-derived word for shrewd; its comparative ends in -ier.
explanation.definitionFit: Canny means shrewd and careful, so the comparative form means shrewder or sharper.

clue.text: Ordered tap: espionage involves paperwork

indicators.note: to involve is to include or contain, so the run of words holds the solution within it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Authorising a wiretap for spying requires forms to be filled in.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon breaks the surface into two statements, hiding that the letters run straight through it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the idiom for excessive bureaucratic forms and official procedure that slow things down.

clue.text: Aid a gullible person, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a sucker is someone easily fooled

explanation.surface: Helping out someone easily duped, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech the final R is silent, so both words are pronounced the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Succour is help or relief given in time of hardship, a formal word for assistance.

clue.text: Imbecile parking Ford in the middle o' Japanese city

indicators.note: the middle is the centre, so only the central letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: a sap is a fool
P is the road-sign symbol for parking
the two central letters of the four
taken as written, the clipped 'of'

explanation.surface: A fool leaving a Ford car in the centre of a Japanese city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the middle o'' looks like it places the car in the city, but 'o'' supplies a letter itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the capital of Hokkaido, a large northern municipality in Japan known for its beer.

clue.text: One who may be barely crawling?

definitions.text: One who may be barely crawling?

blocks.note: surface reading: hardly able to creep along on hands and knees
setter's reading: swimming front crawl while bare, without a costume

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' seems to mean 'only just' but means 'naked', and 'crawling' is the swimming stroke, not creeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone swimming naked is bare while doing a stroke in the water, as the clue says.

clue.text: In the auditorium, spoils string instrument

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: loot is plunder, the spoils of war

explanation.surface: A stringed instrument ruining the concert in a hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like a verb meaning ruins; it is the noun for stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: The lute is a plucked stringed instrument with a pear-shaped body, popular in Renaissance music.

clue.text: Avails oneself of some porterhouse steak

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the solution is a portion of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A diner helping themselves to a share of the porterhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: A porterhouse is a large cut of beef; the letters straddle the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To avail oneself of something is to take advantage of it, which means employing it.

clue.text: Thought Everyman and deejay regularly falling out

indicators.note: letters dropping out at regular intervals leaves every other one standing

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to themselves as I
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: The setter and a disc jockey keep arguing, which gives one of them a notion.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's pseudonym in the clue means the setter, I or ME. 'Falling out' looks like a quarrel but describes letters dropping away.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion or concept formed in the mind is a thought, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Chatshow guests, perhaps doddery actor and nurse

indicators.note: someone doddery is shaky and unsteady, so these letters wobble into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly, unsteady performer and a carer appearing on a talk show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that talk-show guests are just one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Raconteurs are skilled storytellers, the kind of entertaining anecdotalists television hosts invite onto the sofa.

clue.text: Quality of a wine that may be inappropriately picked

blocks.note: first meaning: the bouquet or aroma of a wine
second meaning: the body part people are told not to pick

explanation.surface: A vintage harvested at the wrong time loses its character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked' suggests grapes harvested badly; the second meaning is a rude childhood habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine tasters call a wine's aroma its bouquet, and the facial feature is famously picked in public.

clue.text: Losing energy, De Niro jeers, barking pointed responses

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter is removed
barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go crazy into a new order

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flagging Robert De Niro shouts sharp comebacks at hecklers.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking, short for barking mad, is British slang for crazy. One of the three Es goes before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A rejoinder is a sharp or witty reply, especially a retort to criticism or an argument.
